igcse-0580-inequalities-one-sided-number.description: Read and draw a ray using its boundary, direction and open or filled circle.

sections.title: What do the words tell me about the boundary?
sections.label: Choose strict or inclusive
sections.intro: Identify the value that separates the allowed values from the others. Then decide whether that value itself is allowed.

blocks.html: ‘Less than’ and ‘greater than’ exclude the boundary. ‘At most’ and ‘at least’ include it. For example, ‘at most 4’ is \(x\leq 4\).

blocks.title: Turn words into a one-sided inequality
blocks.prompt: Write an inequality for the statement ‘\(x\) is at most \(0\)’.
blocks.hint: Decide if the boundary counts before choosing a sign.
blocks.solution:
Use \(0\) as the boundary.

The word ‘at’ allows equality.

The inequality is \(x\leq 0\).

blocks.html: ‘At least 4’ includes 4 and values greater than 4. It does not start just after 4.

blocks.title: Read a ray and an endpoint
blocks.prompt: Write the inequality shown by the number line.
blocks.hint: Read the direction of the ray and check whether the circle is filled.
blocks.solution:
The circle is at \(4\). A open circle means excluded.

The arrow runs right, towards greater values. The inequality is \(x\gt 4\).

blocks.html: Read the question aloud and ask whether you would accept the boundary value.

sections.title: Which way does the ray go?
sections.label: Read circles and direction
sections.intro: The line shows a range of real numbers. A ray marks all points on one side of a boundary, including values between the labelled integers.

blocks.html: Use an open circle for \(\lt,\ \gt\) and a filled circle for \(\leq,\ \geq\). Mark a ray towards smaller numbers for less than, and towards greater numbers for more than.

figure.alt: A number line has a filled circle at -2, with an arrow extending to the right.
figure.caption: The filled circle includes −2. The ray extends through all larger numbers.

blocks.title: Represent an inequality on a number line
blocks.prompt: Choose the number-line description of \(x\leq 1\). Place the circle at \(1\).
blocks.hint: The circle shows whether the boundary is included. The ray shows all values on the correct side.
blocks.solution:
First mark the boundary \(1\). Filled circle and an arrow to the left.

The result is shown here.

options.A: Open circle and an arrow to the left.
options.B: Filled circle and an arrow to the right.
options.C: Filled circle and an arrow to the left.

blocks.html: The arrow shows the direction of the allowed numbers. An open circle describes the endpoint only.

blocks.title: Decide which listed values satisfy a ray
blocks.prompt: From \(1, 3, 5\), give all values that satisfy \(x\geq 3\).
blocks.hint: Test each value in the original inequality, including the endpoint.
blocks.solution:
Compare each listed value with \(3\).

The boundary can be included. The values from the list are \(\left\{3, 5\right\}\).

blocks.html: Mark the circle first. Then choose a simple value that should be included and point the ray towards it.

sections.title: What if the variable is written second?
sections.label: Rewrite the same relationship
sections.intro: Read the comparison in the order written. If you put the two sides in the opposite order, change the direction of the sign.

blocks.html: The statements \(-2\lt x\) and \(x\gt -2\) describe the same values. If the original sign includes equality, keep equality when swapping sides.

blocks.title: Read a statement with the variable on the right
blocks.prompt: Rewrite \(2\geq x\) with \(x\) first.
blocks.hint: Swapping the sides preserves the same comparison only when the sign points the other way.
blocks.solution:
The sign in \(2\geq x\) compares \(2\) with \(x\).

When the order of the two sides is swapped, the sign is read the other way. Include equality exactly as before: \(x\leq 2\).

blocks.html: The negative sign of a boundary does not reverse the ray. Compare the actual values on the line.

blocks.title: Write the inequality under an arrow
blocks.prompt: Read the number line and give the inequality for its marked values.
blocks.hint: Look at which side is marked first. Then interpret the circle.
blocks.solution:
Use the scale to read the endpoint \(-3\).

The marked values are on the smaller side and the boundary is excluded, giving \(x\lt -3\).

blocks.html: Test a number on either side when checking a rewritten sign.

examples.title: Turn words into a one-sided inequality
examples.question: Write an inequality for the statement ‘\(x\) is less than \(4\)’.
solution: Use \(4\) as the boundary.
The wording excludes the boundary.
The inequality is \(x\lt 4\).

examples.title: Read a ray and an endpoint
examples.question: Write the inequality shown by the number line.
solution: The circle is at \(-2\). A filled circle means included.
The arrow runs left, towards lower values. The inequality is \(x\leq -2\).

examples.title: Represent an inequality on a number line
examples.question:
Choose the number-line description of \(x\gt -3\). Place the circle at \(-3\).

  1. Open circle and an arrow to the right.
  2. Filled circle and an arrow to the right.
  3. Open circle and an arrow to the left.
solution: First mark the boundary \(-3\). Open circle and an arrow to the right.
The result is shown here.

examples.title: Decide which listed values satisfy a ray
examples.question: From \(0, 2, 4\), give all values that satisfy \(x\gt 2\).
solution: Compare each listed value with \(2\).
The boundary cannot be included. The values from the list are \(\left\{4\right\}\).

examples.title: Read a statement with the variable on the right
examples.question: Rewrite \(-4\gt x\) with \(x\) first.
solution: The sign in \(-4\gt x\) compares \(-4\) with \(x\).
When the order of the two sides is swapped, the sign is read the other way. Include equality exactly as before: \(x\lt -4\).

examples.title: Write the inequality under an arrow
examples.question: Read the number line and give the inequality for its marked values.
solution: Use the scale to read the endpoint \(2\).
The marked values are on the greater side and the boundary is included, giving \(x\geq 2\).

extraPractice.title: Turn words into a one-sided inequality
extraPractice.prompt: Write an inequality for the statement ‘\(x\) is greater than \(3\)’.
extraPractice.hint: Decide if the boundary counts before choosing a sign.
extraPractice.solution:
Use \(3\) as the boundary.

The word ‘at’ allows equality.

The inequality is \(x\gt 3\).

extraPractice.title: Read a ray and an endpoint
extraPractice.prompt: Write the inequality shown by the number line.
extraPractice.hint: Read the direction of the ray and check whether the circle is filled.
extraPractice.solution:
The circle is at \(1\). A open circle means excluded.

The arrow runs left, towards lower values. The inequality is \(x\lt 1\).

extraPractice.title: Represent an inequality on a number line
extraPractice.prompt: Choose the number-line description of \(x\geq 4\). Place the circle at \(4\).
extraPractice.hint: The circle shows whether the boundary is included. The ray shows all values on the correct side.
extraPractice.solution:
First mark the boundary \(4\). Filled circle and an arrow to the right.

The result is shown here.

options.A: Filled circle and an arrow to the left.
options.B: Filled circle and an arrow to the right.
options.C: Open circle and an arrow to the right.

extraPractice.title: Decide which listed values satisfy a ray
extraPractice.prompt: From \(-3, -1, 1\), give all values that satisfy \(x\lt -1\).
extraPractice.hint: Test each value in the original inequality, including the endpoint.
extraPractice.solution:
Compare each listed value with \(-1\).

The boundary cannot be included. The values from the list are \(\left\{-3\right\}\).

extraPractice.title: Read a statement with the variable on the right
extraPractice.prompt: Rewrite \(3\lt x\) with \(x\) first.
extraPractice.hint: Swapping the sides preserves the same comparison only when the sign points the other way.
extraPractice.solution:
The sign in \(3\lt x\) compares \(3\) with \(x\).

When the order of the two sides is swapped, the sign is read the other way. Include equality exactly as before: \(x\gt 3\).

extraPractice.title: Write the inequality under an arrow
extraPractice.prompt: Read the number line and give the inequality for its marked values.
extraPractice.hint: Look at which side is marked first. Then interpret the circle.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the scale to read the endpoint \(4\).

The marked values are on the greater side and the boundary is excluded, giving \(x\gt 4\).

glossary.definition: The value where a ray starts or stops.
The boundary is excluded.
The boundary is included.
A line starting at a point and extending in one direction.
Any value on the number line.

revision.body:
Choose strict or inclusive

‘Less than’ and ‘greater than’ exclude the boundary. ‘At most’ and ‘at least’ include it. For example, ‘at most 4’ is \(x\leq 4\).

Read circles and direction

Use an open circle for \(\lt,\ \gt\) and a filled circle for \(\leq,\ \geq\). Mark a ray towards smaller numbers for less than, and towards greater numbers for more than.

Rewrite the same relationship

The statements \(-2\lt x\) and \(x\gt -2\) describe the same values. If the original sign includes equality, keep equality when swapping sides.

Example

‘More than −3’ gives \(x\gt -3\). Use an open circle at −3 and draw the ray to the right.

Check yourself

  • Write ‘at most 2’ as an inequality in x.
  • Does −4 satisfy \(x\lt -3\)?

Answers \(x\leq 2\) and yes, because \(-4\lt -3\).
revision.checks:
• ‘At least 4’ includes 4 and values greater than 4. It does not start just after 4.
  • The arrow shows the direction of the allowed numbers. An open circle describes the endpoint only.
  • The negative sign of a boundary does not reverse the ray. Compare the actual values on the line.
revision.examTip: Test a number on either side when checking a rewritten sign.

igcse-0580-inequalities-bounded-number-l.description: Read two endpoint types, write one chained range and identify the integers it contains.

sections.title: How do I read two boundaries together?
sections.label: A lower and an upper bound
sections.intro: A segment shows values between two endpoints. Each circle tells you separately whether its own endpoint is included.

blocks.html: The left boundary goes first in a chained inequality. For example, \(-1\leq x\lt 4\) means x is at least −1 and less than 4.

figure.alt: A number line has a filled circle at -2 and a open circle at 3, joined by a segment.
figure.caption: The highlighted range starts at an included endpoint and ends at an excluded endpoint.

blocks.title: Read a bounded solution from a number line
blocks.prompt: Give the single inequality in x shown on the number line.
blocks.hint: Treat the two circles independently. The values must satisfy both bounds.
blocks.solution:
Read left to right between \(-3\) and \(1\). The segment requires both conditions.

The left boundary is excluded. The right boundary is included. Write \(-3\lt x\leq 1\).

blocks.html: A filled circle on one end says nothing about the other end. Read the two signs separately.

blocks.title: Translate two limits into one inequality
blocks.prompt: A reading \(x\) is greater than \(0\) and at most \(6\). Write its range.
blocks.hint: Read ‘and’ as two conditions on the same quantity.
blocks.solution:
The lower condition is \(x\gt 0\). The upper one is \(x\leq 6\).

Join both with the smaller boundary first to obtain \(0\lt x\leq 6\).

blocks.html: Say the lower condition and upper condition as two short sentences before joining them.

sections.title: What does ‘and’ mean for a range?
sections.label: Use only the common values
sections.intro: A value must satisfy both conditions joined by ‘and’. It lies in the common part of the two rays.

blocks.html: The conditions \(x\gt -3\) and \(x\leq 2\) are both true on \(-3\lt x\leq 2\). Draw only that segment and its correct circles.

blocks.title: Combine two inequalities using and
blocks.prompt: Write one inequality to show that \(x\gt -2\) and \(x\leq 2\).
blocks.hint: The same x must satisfy both statements.
blocks.solution:
Start at the left boundary \(-2\). Rewrite the lower condition with this number first.

Follow the number line to the right boundary \(2\). Keep both endpoint conditions: \(-2\lt x\leq 2\).

blocks.html: Marking both entire rays would include values that satisfy just one of the limits.

blocks.title: List the integer values within bounds
blocks.prompt: List every integer \(x\) that satisfies \(-1\lt x\leq 5\).
blocks.hint: Use the signs to decide whether to include each boundary integer.
blocks.solution:
Start with the smallest allowed integer, \(0\). Walk right one integer at a time.

Stop at \(5\). The complete list is \(\left\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\right\}\).

blocks.html: Check an interior value and each endpoint against both of the original conditions.

sections.title: How do I list only the allowed integers?
sections.label: Start at the first valid integer
sections.intro: A range normally includes real numbers. When an answer asks for integers, select only the whole-number points that satisfy the range.

blocks.html: For \(-2\leq x\lt 3\), the integers are \(-2,\,-1,\,0,\,1,\,2\). Zero is an integer, and the open right endpoint excludes 3.

blocks.title: Check each candidate against both bounds
blocks.prompt: From \(-2,\quad -1,\quad \frac{3}{2},\quad 4,\quad 5\), give every value that satisfies \(-1\lt x\leq 4\).
blocks.hint: Check the lower condition and the upper condition for each candidate.
blocks.solution:
The first and last candidates lie outside the interval. \(\frac{3}{2}\) lies strictly inside it.

Test the endpoints against their own signs. The allowed candidates are \(\left\{\frac{3}{2}, 4\right\}\).

blocks.html: For a non-integer bound, avoid rounding it and accidentally including the wrong integer. Move to the first actual integer inside the interval.

blocks.title: Choose the two endpoints for a bounded segment
blocks.prompt: For \(-4\lt x\leq -1\), which circles are needed at the two boundaries?
blocks.hint: Open means the endpoint is excluded. Filled means it is included.
blocks.solution:
Left circle open, right filled. Join them with a segment.

Join the two boundary values because every real value between them satisfies both conditions.

blocks.html: Read the lower and upper signs before writing a list. Check there is no missing integer between your first and last.

examples.title: Read a bounded solution from a number line
examples.question: Give the single inequality in x shown on the number line.
solution: Read left to right between \(-2\) and \(1\). The segment requires both conditions.
The left boundary is included. The right boundary is excluded. Write \(-2\leq x\lt 1\).

examples.title: Translate two limits into one inequality
examples.question: A reading \(x\) is at least \(-1\) and less than \(4\). Write its range.
solution: The lower condition is \(x\geq -1\). The upper one is \(x\lt 4\).
Join both with the smaller boundary first to obtain \(-1\leq x\lt 4\).

examples.title: Combine two inequalities using and
examples.question: Write one inequality to show that \(x\geq -4\) and \(x\lt -1\).
solution: Start at the left boundary \(-4\). Rewrite the lower condition with this number first.
Follow the number line to the right boundary \(-1\). Keep both endpoint conditions: \(-4\leq x\lt -1\).

examples.title: List the integer values within bounds
examples.question: List every integer \(x\) that satisfies \(1\leq x\lt 6\).
solution: Start with the smallest allowed integer, \(1\). Walk right one integer at a time.
Stop at \(5\). The complete list is \(\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\right\}\).

examples.title: Check each candidate against both bounds
examples.question: From \(-4,\quad -3,\quad -1,\quad 1,\quad 2\), give every value that satisfies \(-3\leq x\lt 1\).
solution: The first and last candidates lie outside the interval. \(-1\) lies strictly inside it.
Test the endpoints against their own signs. The allowed candidates are \(\left\{-3, -1\right\}\).

examples.title: Choose the two endpoints for a bounded segment
examples.question:
For \(0\leq x\lt 6\), which circles are needed at the two boundaries?

  1. Both circles filled
  2. Left circle filled, right open
  3. Left circle open, right filled
  4. Both circles open
solution: Left circle filled, right open. Join them with a segment.
Join the two boundary values because every real value between them satisfies both conditions.

extraPractice.title: Read a bounded solution from a number line
extraPractice.prompt: Give the single inequality in x shown on the number line.
extraPractice.hint: Treat the two circles independently. The values must satisfy both bounds.
extraPractice.solution:
Read left to right between \(-1\) and \(4\). The segment requires both conditions.

The left boundary is excluded. The right boundary is excluded. Write \(-1\lt x\lt 4\).

extraPractice.title: Translate two limits into one inequality
extraPractice.prompt: A reading \(x\) is greater than \(-4\) and less than \(-1\). Write its range.
extraPractice.hint: Read ‘and’ as two conditions on the same quantity.
extraPractice.solution:
The lower condition is \(x\gt -4\). The upper one is \(x\lt -1\).

Join both with the smaller boundary first to obtain \(-4\lt x\lt -1\).

extraPractice.title: Combine two inequalities using and
extraPractice.prompt: Write one inequality to show that \(x\gt 1\) and \(x\lt 6\).
extraPractice.hint: The same x must satisfy both statements.
extraPractice.solution:
Start at the left boundary \(1\). Rewrite the lower condition with this number first.

Follow the number line to the right boundary \(6\). Keep both endpoint conditions: \(1\lt x\lt 6\).

extraPractice.title: List the integer values within bounds
extraPractice.prompt: List every integer \(x\) that satisfies \(-2\lt x\lt 1\).
extraPractice.hint: Use the signs to decide whether to include each boundary integer.
extraPractice.solution:
Start with the smallest allowed integer, \(-1\). Walk right one integer at a time.

Stop at \(0\). The complete list is \(\left\{-1, 0\right\}\).

extraPractice.title: Check each candidate against both bounds
extraPractice.prompt: From \(-1,\quad 0,\quad 3,\quad 6,\quad 7\), give every value that satisfies \(0\lt x\lt 6\).
extraPractice.hint: Check the lower condition and the upper condition for each candidate.
extraPractice.solution:
The first and last candidates lie outside the interval. \(3\) lies strictly inside it.

Test the endpoints against their own signs. The allowed candidates are \(\left\{3\right\}\).

extraPractice.title: Choose the two endpoints for a bounded segment
extraPractice.prompt: For \(-2\lt x\lt 2\), which circles are needed at the two boundaries?
extraPractice.hint: Open means the endpoint is excluded. Filled means it is included.
extraPractice.solution:
Both circles open. Join them with a segment.

Join the two boundary values because every real value between them satisfies both conditions.

glossary.definition: The endpoint on the smaller side.
The endpoint on the greater side.
A part of a line between two points.
The values that satisfy both conditions.
A positive or negative whole number, including zero.

revision.body:
A lower and an upper bound

The left boundary goes first in a chained inequality. For example, \(-1\leq x\lt 4\) means x is at least −1 and less than 4.

Use only the common values

The conditions \(x\gt -3\) and \(x\leq 2\) are both true on \(-3\lt x\leq 2\). Draw only that segment and its correct circles.

Start at the first valid integer

For \(-2\leq x\lt 3\), the integers are \(-2,\,-1,\,0,\,1,\,2\). Zero is an integer, and the open right endpoint excludes 3.

Example

The integers satisfying \(-1\lt x\leq 3\) are \(0,\,1,\,2,\,3\).

Check yourself

  • Combine \(x\geq -4\) and \(x\lt 1\) as one inequality.
  • List every integer satisfying \(0\lt x\leq 4\).

Answers \(-4\leq x\lt 1\) and \(1,\,2,\,3,\,4\).
revision.checks:
• A filled circle on one end says nothing about the other end. Read the two signs separately.
  • Marking both entire rays would include values that satisfy just one of the limits.
  • For a non-integer bound, avoid rounding it and accidentally including the wrong integer. Move to the first actual integer inside the interval.
revision.examTip: Read the lower and upper signs before writing a list. Check there is no missing integer between your first and last.

igcse-0580-inequalities-solving-linear.description: Isolate a variable and reverse the inequality exactly when multiplying or dividing by a negative.

sections.title: Which operations preserve the direction?
sections.label: Use inverse operations
sections.intro: Add or subtract the same amount on both sides to keep the comparison true for the same values. A positive scale factor also preserves order.

blocks.html: For \(5x+2\lt 17\), subtract 2 and divide by 5. You get \(x\lt 3\). Keep the strict sign through both operations.

blocks.title: Solve an inequality with a positive coefficient
blocks.prompt: Solve \(3x+4\lt \frac{23}{2}\). Give the whole solution.
blocks.hint: Use the inverse operations in order. Dividing by a positive number keeps the sign.
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(4\) from both sides to get \(3x\lt \frac{15}{2}\).

Divide by positive \(3\). The inequality sign keeps the same direction.

Write the final range as \(x\lt \frac{5}{2}\).

blocks.html: The result is a range of x-values. A single value at the boundary is not a complete answer.

blocks.title: Solve an inequality with brackets
blocks.prompt: Solve \(4\left(x-3\right)\lt -4\). Give the whole solution.
blocks.hint: A positive factor outside the brackets can be divided away before opening them.
blocks.solution:
Divide both sides by \(4\) to isolate the bracket and get \(x-3\lt -1\).

Add \(3\) to both sides.

Write the final range as \(x\lt 2\).

blocks.html: After solving, substitute a value inside the range to check the direction.

sections.title: Why does a negative multiplier reverse the sign?
sections.label: Reverse order for negative scaling
sections.intro: On the number line, multiplying by −1 reflects the values about zero. The order changes even when the original two numbers were both positive.

blocks.html: From \(9\gt 4\) comes \(-9\lt -4\). Follow the same rule when dividing by a negative number. Keep the presence or absence of equality.

figure.alt: A number line has a open circle at 2, with an arrow extending to the right.
figure.caption: A strict lower bound at 2 leaves 2 out and keeps all larger values.

blocks.title: Reverse the sign when dividing by a negative
blocks.prompt: Solve \(-3x+5\geq -1\). Give the whole solution.
blocks.hint: A negative divisor reverses the order of two numbers.
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(5\) to get \(-3x\geq -6\).

Divide by \(-3\). Reverse the inequality sign because the divisor is negative.

Write the final range as \(x\leq 2\).

blocks.html: Adding or subtracting a negative amount does not reverse a sign. Reversal is for multiplying or dividing by a negative number.

blocks.title: Collect variable terms from both sides
blocks.prompt: Solve \(3x+9\gt 6x+3\). Give the whole solution.
blocks.hint: Move the smaller variable term first so its new coefficient is positive.
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(3x\) from both sides and then subtract \(3\). The result is \(6\gt 3x\).

Divide by positive \(3\). Rewriting with \(x\) first requires swapping the sides and the written direction.

Write the final range as \(x\lt 2\).

blocks.html: If the variable has a negative coefficient, you can move that term to the other side first and work with a positive coefficient.

sections.title: How do I solve with variables on both sides?
sections.label: Collect the variable terms
sections.intro: If x appears twice, bring the variable terms together and the numbers together. Keep each whole side of the inequality consistent.

blocks.html: Move the smaller x-coefficient first to obtain a positive variable term when possible. Clear positive denominators before collecting terms if that simplifies the working.

blocks.title: Clear a positive denominator
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\frac{4x-3}{3}\lt 3\). Give the whole solution.
blocks.hint: Multiply all of both sides by the positive denominator first.
blocks.solution:
Multiply by \(3\) to get \(4x-3\lt 9\). Keep the sign because the denominator is positive.

Add \(3\) and then divide by \(4\).

Write the final range as \(x\lt 3\).

blocks.html: If you exchange the complete left and right sides to write x first, reverse the written comparison so it still states the same order.

blocks.title: Find when one expression is smaller
blocks.prompt: For what values of \(x\) is \(3x+10\) less than \(5x+4\)?
blocks.hint: Translate the words into an inequality before isolating the unknown.
blocks.solution:
‘Less than’ gives \(3x+10\lt 5x+4\).

Subtract \(3x+4\). This gives \(6\lt 2x\). Divide by 2 and rewrite with x first: \(x\gt 3\).

blocks.html: Show the calculation just before your final sign. A quick test at a candidate value can catch a reversed comparison.

examples.title: Solve an inequality with a positive coefficient
examples.question: Solve \(2x+3\leq 6\). Give the whole solution.
solution: Subtract \(3\) from both sides to get \(2x\leq 3\).
Divide by positive \(2\). The inequality sign keeps the same direction.
Write the final range as \(x\leq \frac{3}{2}\).

examples.title: Solve an inequality with brackets
examples.question: Solve \(3\left(x-2\right)\geq -\frac{3}{2}\). Give the whole solution.
solution: Divide both sides by \(3\) to isolate the bracket and get \(x-2\geq -\frac{1}{2}\).
Add \(2\) to both sides.
Write the final range as \(x\geq \frac{3}{2}\).

examples.title: Reverse the sign when dividing by a negative
examples.question: Solve \(-2x+4\lt 1\). Give the whole solution.
solution: Subtract \(4\) to get \(-2x\lt -3\).
Divide by \(-2\). Reverse the inequality sign because the divisor is negative.
Write the final range as \(x\gt \frac{3}{2}\).

examples.title: Collect variable terms from both sides
examples.question: Solve \(2x+\frac{16}{3}\leq 4x+2\). Give the whole solution.
solution: Subtract \(2x\) from both sides and then subtract \(2\). The result is \(\frac{10}{3}\leq 2x\).
Divide by positive \(2\). Rewriting with \(x\) first requires swapping the sides and the written direction.
Write the final range as \(x\geq \frac{5}{3}\).

examples.title: Clear a positive denominator
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{3x-2}{2}\geq 2\). Give the whole solution.
solution: Multiply by \(2\) to get \(3x-2\geq 4\). Keep the sign because the denominator is positive.
Add \(2\) and then divide by \(3\).
Write the final range as \(x\geq 2\).

examples.title: Find when one expression is smaller
examples.question: For what values of \(x\) is \(2x+7\) less than \(4x+3\)?
solution: ‘Less than’ gives \(2x+7\lt 4x+3\).
Subtract \(2x+3\). This gives \(4\lt 2x\). Divide by 2 and rewrite with x first: \(x\gt 2\).

extraPractice.title: Solve an inequality with a positive coefficient
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(4x+5\geq 19\). Give the whole solution.
extraPractice.hint: Use the inverse operations in order. Dividing by a positive number keeps the sign.
extraPractice.solution:
Subtract \(5\) from both sides to get \(4x\geq 14\).

Divide by positive \(4\). The inequality sign keeps the same direction.

Write the final range as \(x\geq \frac{7}{2}\).

extraPractice.title: Solve an inequality with brackets
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(5\left(x-4\right)\gt -\frac{15}{2}\). Give the whole solution.
extraPractice.hint: A positive factor outside the brackets can be divided away before opening them.
extraPractice.solution:
Divide both sides by \(5\) to isolate the bracket and get \(x-4\gt -\frac{3}{2}\).

Add \(4\) to both sides.

Write the final range as \(x\gt \frac{5}{2}\).

extraPractice.title: Reverse the sign when dividing by a negative
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(-4x+6\leq -4\). Give the whole solution.
extraPractice.hint: A negative divisor reverses the order of two numbers.
extraPractice.solution:
Subtract \(6\) to get \(-4x\leq -10\).

Divide by \(-4\). Reverse the inequality sign because the divisor is negative.

Write the final range as \(x\geq \frac{5}{2}\).

extraPractice.title: Collect variable terms from both sides
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(4x+\frac{40}{3}\lt 8x+4\). Give the whole solution.
extraPractice.hint: Move the smaller variable term first so its new coefficient is positive.
extraPractice.solution:
Subtract \(4x\) from both sides and then subtract \(4\). The result is \(\frac{28}{3}\lt 4x\).

Divide by positive \(4\). Rewriting with \(x\) first requires swapping the sides and the written direction.

Write the final range as \(x\gt \frac{7}{3}\).

extraPractice.title: Clear a positive denominator
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\frac{5x-4}{4}\leq 4\). Give the whole solution.
extraPractice.hint: Multiply all of both sides by the positive denominator first.
extraPractice.solution:
Multiply by \(4\) to get \(5x-4\leq 16\). Keep the sign because the denominator is positive.

Add \(4\) and then divide by \(5\).

Write the final range as \(x\leq 4\).

extraPractice.title: Find when one expression is smaller
extraPractice.prompt: For what values of \(x\) is \(4x+13\) less than \(6x+5\)?
extraPractice.hint: Translate the words into an inequality before isolating the unknown.
extraPractice.solution:
‘Less than’ gives \(4x+13\lt 6x+5\).

Subtract \(4x+5\). This gives \(8\lt 2x\). Divide by 2 and rewrite with x first: \(x\gt 4\).

glossary.definition: An inequality where the variable has degree one.
An operation that reverses a previous one.
The multiplier of a variable.
Rewrite so that the variable is on its own.
Multiply by the same factor.

revision.body:
Use inverse operations

For \(5x+2\lt 17\), subtract 2 and divide by 5. You get \(x\lt 3\). Keep the strict sign through both operations.

Reverse order for negative scaling

From \(9\gt 4\) comes \(-9\lt -4\). Follow the same rule when dividing by a negative number. Keep the presence or absence of equality.

Collect the variable terms

Move the smaller x-coefficient first to obtain a positive variable term when possible. Clear positive denominators before collecting terms if that simplifies the working.

Example

\(-4x+7\lt -1\) gives \(-4x\lt -8\). Dividing by −4 gives \(x\gt 2\).

Check yourself

  • Solve \(6x-3\leq 18\).
  • Solve \(-3x+5\gt 14\).

Answers \(x\leq \frac{7}{2}\) and \(x\lt -3\).
revision.checks:
• The result is a range of x-values. A single value at the boundary is not a complete answer.
  • Adding or subtracting a negative amount does not reverse a sign. Reversal is for multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
  • If you exchange the complete left and right sides to write x first, reverse the written comparison so it still states the same order.
revision.examTip: Show the calculation just before your final sign. A quick test at a candidate value can catch a reversed comparison.

igcse-0580-inequalities-chained-inequali.description: Solve both parts of a chained inequality and interpret the bounds in contexts such as budgets.

sections.title: What should I do to all three parts?
sections.label: Apply one operation throughout
sections.intro: A chain compares its middle expression to two different bounds. Applying the same inverse operation to all three expressions is a compact way to solve both comparisons.

blocks.html: From \(1\leq 2x+3\lt 9\), subtract 3 throughout and divide by 2. The result is \(-1\leq x\lt 3\).

figure.alt: A number line has a filled circle at -1 and a open circle at 3, joined by a segment.
figure.caption: After solving, keep the same two endpoint decisions when you represent the range.

blocks.title: Solve a chained inequality by acting on all three parts
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\frac{5}{2}\lt 3x+4\lt \frac{35}{2}\).
blocks.hint: Apply the same operation to the left, middle and right expressions.
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(4\) from all three expressions.

Divide all three by \(3\). The coefficient is positive, so both signs stay the same. The answer is \(-\frac{1}{2}\lt x\lt \frac{9}{2}\).

blocks.html: Subtracting a number only from the middle expression changes the conditions.

blocks.title: Reverse both signs in a decreasing chain
blocks.hint: A negative divisor affects both comparisons. Keep track of which endpoint retains equality.
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(5\) throughout. Then divide all three expressions by \(-3\).

Reverse both signs to get \(4\geq x\gt -\frac{1}{2}\).

Read from the smaller boundary first to write \(-\frac{1}{2}\lt x\leq 4\).

blocks.html: An alternative is to split the chain into two inequalities. Solve each one and take the intersection.

sections.title: What happens if the middle coefficient is negative?
sections.label: Reverse both comparisons
sections.intro: A negative divisor reverses the left comparison and the right comparison. The resulting chain can be written with the greater number first.

blocks.html: When rewriting the result from the lower endpoint to the upper endpoint, use the inclusivity signs that belong to those same endpoint values.

blocks.title: Clear a denominator in a chained inequality
blocks.prompt: Solve \(1\lt \frac{x+4}{3}\leq \frac{8}{3}\).
blocks.hint: Clear the denominator in all three parts before moving the constant.
blocks.solution:
Multiply all three parts by \(3\). This is positive, so the signs remain unchanged.

Subtract \(4\) from all three parts to obtain \(-1\lt x\leq 4\).

blocks.html: One inequality may be strict while the other is inclusive. Check that each endpoint still has its own type after changing direction.

blocks.title: Find the integers in a solved range
blocks.prompt: List the integer values of \(x\) that satisfy \(0\lt 3x+3\lt 12\).
blocks.hint: First solve the inequality for real numbers. Then keep only the integers it contains.
blocks.solution:
Solve the chain by subtracting \(3\) throughout and dividing by \(3\), giving \(-1\lt x\lt 3\).

List the integers starting at \(0\) and ending at \(2\): \(\left\{0, 1, 2\right\}\).

blocks.html: Try both boundary values in the original chain. Only the included one should pass if the signs differ.

sections.title: How do I turn a range into a usable result?
sections.label: Interpret least and greatest integers
sections.intro: The answer to a real-valued inequality can be a range. The requested number of objects may be restricted to whole numbers.

blocks.html: For a maximum budget, find the largest allowed integer. For a minimum total, choose the smallest allowed integer. The sign tells you what to do if a boundary is itself a whole number.

blocks.title: Form a budget inequality and find a whole number
blocks.prompt: A print order costs £7 to set up and £5 per poster. The budget is at most £28. Find the greatest number of posters that can be ordered.
blocks.hint: Form an inequality including the fixed charge before deciding how to round.
blocks.solution:
Let \(x\) count posters. The budget gives \(5x+7\leq 28\), with \(x\) a non-negative integer.

Subtract the set-up price and divide by the price per poster: \(x\leq \frac{21}{5}\).

The largest allowed integer is \(4\). The next integer exceeds the budget.

blocks.html: Ordinary rounding can violate the requirement. A bound of \(x\geq 4.1\) requires at least five whole units.

blocks.title: Find the least acceptable whole-number amount
blocks.prompt: A club already has 6 tablets. Each box contains 4 more. It needs at least 24 tablets altogether. Find the least number of boxes it should obtain.
blocks.hint: At least means equal to or greater. Pick the first allowed whole number after solving.
blocks.solution:
Let \(x\) be the number of boxes. The model is \(4x+6\geq 24\).

Subtract \(6\) and divide by \(4\): \(x\geq \frac{9}{2}\).

The smallest integer that satisfies the minimum is \(5\).

blocks.html: Check the chosen integer and its nearest relevant neighbour against the original requirement.

examples.title: Solve a chained inequality by acting on all three parts
examples.question: Solve \(1\leq 2x+3\leq 11\).
solution: Subtract \(3\) from all three expressions.
Divide all three by \(2\). The coefficient is positive, so both signs stay the same. The answer is \(-1\leq x\leq 4\).

examples.title: Reverse both signs in a decreasing chain
examples.question: Solve \(-3\lt -2x+4\leq 6\).
solution: Subtract \(4\) throughout. Then divide all three expressions by \(-2\).
Reverse both signs to get \(\frac{7}{2}\gt x\geq -1\).
Read from the smaller boundary first to write \(-1\leq x\lt \frac{7}{2}\).

examples.title: Clear a denominator in a chained inequality
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{1}{2}\leq \frac{x+3}{2}\lt \frac{5}{2}\).
solution: Multiply all three parts by \(2\). This is positive, so the signs remain unchanged.
Subtract \(3\) from all three parts to obtain \(-2\leq x\lt 2\).

examples.title: Find the integers in a solved range
examples.question: List the integer values of \(x\) that satisfy \(-1\leq 2x+2\leq 6\).
solution: Solve the chain by subtracting \(2\) throughout and dividing by \(2\), giving \(-\frac{3}{2}\leq x\leq 2\).
List the integers starting at \(-1\) and ending at \(2\): \(\left\{-1, 0, 1, 2\right\}\).

examples.title: Form a budget inequality and find a whole number
examples.question: A print order costs £6 to set up and £4 per poster. The budget is at most £18. Find the greatest number of posters that can be ordered.
solution: Let \(x\) count posters. The budget gives \(4x+6\leq 18\), with \(x\) a non-negative integer.
Subtract the set-up price and divide by the price per poster: \(x\leq 3\).
The largest allowed integer is \(3\). The next integer exceeds the budget.

examples.title: Find the least acceptable whole-number amount
examples.question: A club already has 5 tablets. Each box contains 3 more. It needs at least 15 tablets altogether. Find the least number of boxes it should obtain.
solution: Let \(x\) be the number of boxes. The model is \(3x+5\geq 15\).
Subtract \(5\) and divide by \(3\): \(x\geq \frac{10}{3}\).
The smallest integer that satisfies the minimum is \(4\).

extraPractice.title: Solve a chained inequality by acting on all three parts
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(5\leq 4x+5\lt 25\).
extraPractice.hint: Apply the same operation to the left, middle and right expressions.
extraPractice.solution:
Subtract \(5\) from all three expressions.

Divide all three by \(4\). The coefficient is positive, so both signs stay the same. The answer is \(0\leq x\lt 5\).

extraPractice.title: Reverse both signs in a decreasing chain
extraPractice.hint: A negative divisor affects both comparisons. Keep track of which endpoint retains equality.
extraPractice.solution:
Subtract \(6\) throughout. Then divide all three expressions by \(-4\).

Reverse both signs to get \(\frac{9}{2}\gt x\geq 0\).

Read from the smaller boundary first to write \(0\leq x\lt \frac{9}{2}\).

extraPractice.title: Clear a denominator in a chained inequality
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\frac{5}{4}\leq \frac{x+5}{4}\lt \frac{11}{4}\).
extraPractice.hint: Clear the denominator in all three parts before moving the constant.
extraPractice.solution:
Multiply all three parts by \(4\). This is positive, so the signs remain unchanged.

Subtract \(5\) from all three parts to obtain \(0\leq x\lt 6\).

extraPractice.title: Find the integers in a solved range
extraPractice.prompt: List the integer values of \(x\) that satisfy \(2\leq 4x+4\lt 20\).
extraPractice.hint: First solve the inequality for real numbers. Then keep only the integers it contains.
extraPractice.solution:
Solve the chain by subtracting \(4\) throughout and dividing by \(4\), giving \(-\frac{1}{2}\leq x\lt 4\).

List the integers starting at \(0\) and ending at \(3\): \(\left\{0, 1, 2, 3\right\}\).

extraPractice.title: Form a budget inequality and find a whole number
extraPractice.prompt: A print order costs £8 to set up and £6 per poster. The budget is at most £40. Find the greatest number of posters that can be ordered.
extraPractice.hint: Form an inequality including the fixed charge before deciding how to round.
extraPractice.solution:
Let \(x\) count posters. The budget gives \(6x+8\leq 40\), with \(x\) a non-negative integer.

Subtract the set-up price and divide by the price per poster: \(x\leq \frac{16}{3}\).

The largest allowed integer is \(5\). The next integer exceeds the budget.

extraPractice.title: Find the least acceptable whole-number amount
extraPractice.prompt: A club already has 7 tablets. Each box contains 5 more. It needs at least 33 tablets altogether. Find the least number of boxes it should obtain.
extraPractice.hint: At least means equal to or greater. Pick the first allowed whole number after solving.
extraPractice.solution:
Let \(x\) be the number of boxes. The model is \(5x+7\geq 33\).

Subtract \(7\) and divide by \(5\): \(x\geq \frac{26}{5}\).

The smallest integer that satisfies the minimum is \(6\).

glossary.definition: Two inequalities joined through one middle expression.
Applied to the left, middle and right expressions.
A condition that limits the possible values.
The smallest allowed value.
The largest allowed value.

revision.body:
Apply one operation throughout

From \(1\leq 2x+3\lt 9\), subtract 3 throughout and divide by 2. The result is \(-1\leq x\lt 3\).

Reverse both comparisons

When rewriting the result from the lower endpoint to the upper endpoint, use the inclusivity signs that belong to those same endpoint values.

Interpret least and greatest integers

For a maximum budget, find the largest allowed integer. For a minimum total, choose the smallest allowed integer. The sign tells you what to do if a boundary is itself a whole number.

Example

\(0\lt 6-2x\leq 10\) gives \(3\gt x\geq -2\) after subtracting 6 and dividing by −2. Reorder to \(-2\leq x\lt 3\).

Check yourself

  • Solve \(2\leq 3x+5\lt 14\).
  • What is the greatest whole number satisfying \(x\lt 8\)?

Answers \(-1\leq x\lt 3\) and \(7\).
revision.checks:
• Subtracting a number only from the middle expression changes the conditions.
  • One inequality may be strict while the other is inclusive. Check that each endpoint still has its own type after changing direction.
  • Ordinary rounding can violate the requirement. A bound of \(x\geq 4.1\) requires at least five whole units.
revision.examTip: Check the chosen integer and its nearest relevant neighbour against the original requirement.

igcse-0580-inequalities-graph-one-bounda.description: Draw the boundary, choose its line style and shade the unwanted half-plane.

sections.title: What separates the wanted and unwanted sides?
sections.label: Find the boundary and its style
sections.intro: Replace the inequality sign with equality to find a straight boundary line. Plot two suitable points unless the line is horizontal or vertical and you can locate it directly.

blocks.html: Use a solid line for \(\leq\) or \(\geq\). Those signs admit equality. Use a broken line for \(\lt\) or \(\gt\) because the boundary itself is excluded.

blocks.title: Choose how to draw the boundary
blocks.prompt: Which line style is used for the boundary of \(2x+y\geq 3\)?
blocks.hint: A line style only tells whether the boundary itself belongs.
blocks.solution:
Replace the sign with equality to get \(2x+y=3\).

Use a solid boundary because equality is allowed.

blocks.html: The style of the line does not tell you which side to shade. Make the side decision separately.

blocks.title: Read a vertical boundary
blocks.prompt: The shaded part is unwanted. Which inequality describes the clear half-plane?
blocks.hint: A vertical boundary limits x. Check which side is clear and whether the line is broken.
blocks.solution:
The vertical boundary has equation \(x=-1\). Look at x-coordinates, which change left to right.

The clear side is to the left. Use the line type to get \(x\leq -1\).

blocks.html: For \(x=3\), keep x constant to draw a vertical line. For \(y=3\), keep y constant to draw a horizontal line.

sections.title: How do I decide which side fails the inequality?
sections.label: Test a point off the line
sections.intro: An off-line point tells you whether its whole half-plane is wanted. If substitution gives a true statement, that side is wanted.

blocks.html: Cambridge uses shading for the unwanted half-plane unless the question directs otherwise. Shade the other side if your test point satisfies the inequality.

figure.alt: A solid descending line crosses both axes at 3. Its lower-left half-plane is shaded. The origin is marked.
figure.caption: The origin makes x + y less than 3. Shade its side when the condition requires x + y to be at least 3.

blocks.title: Read a horizontal boundary
blocks.prompt: Which condition describes the unshaded part of this graph?
blocks.hint: In a horizontal boundary, the fixed coordinate is y.
blocks.solution:
The horizontal boundary has equation \(y=3\).

The wanted area is above the boundary. The line style gives the inequality \(y\gt 3\).

blocks.html: If the origin lies on the boundary, it cannot distinguish the two sides. Test a different easy point.

blocks.title: Use an off-line point to choose the side
blocks.prompt: For \(2x+y\geq 3\), use \(\left(0,0\right)\) as a test point. Where does it lie?
blocks.hint: Substitute both coordinates and decide whether the comparison is true.
blocks.solution:
The origin is off the line, so it can be used as a test point.

At \(\left(0,0\right)\), the left side has value \(0\). The comparison \(0\geq 3\) is false.

The test point is on the unwanted side.

options.A: The test point is on the unwanted side
options.B: The test point is on the wanted side

blocks.html: Show the two coordinates substituted into the inequality. This checks the side even if the line is steep.

sections.title: How do I read a horizontal, vertical or sloping boundary?
sections.label: Read both direction and equality
sections.intro: For a vertical line compare x-coordinates. For a horizontal line compare y-coordinates. For a sloping line, rearranging the inequality for y may make above or below clear.

blocks.html: Check the equation, then use the wanted side to choose whether the comparison is smaller or greater. Include equality on a solid line only.

blocks.title: Use an off-line point to choose the side
blocks.prompt: For \(2x+y\geq 0\), use \(\left(1,1\right)\) as a test point. Where does it lie?
blocks.hint: Substitute both coordinates and decide whether the comparison is true.
blocks.solution:
The origin is on this boundary, so choose another point.

At \(\left(1,1\right)\), the left side has value \(3\). The comparison \(3\geq 0\) is true.

The test point is on the wanted side.

options.A: The test point is on the unwanted side
options.B: The test point is on the wanted side

blocks.html: The visual edge of the printed grid is not a boundary of the inequality unless the question draws or states it as one.

blocks.title: Choose the unwanted side of a sloping boundary
blocks.prompt: For \(2x+y\gt 4\), which side of the boundary should be shaded using the Cambridge convention?
blocks.hint: First find the satisfying side. Shade the other one.
blocks.solution:
Isolate y in \(2x+y\gt 4\). The wanted region is above the line.

With Cambridge's convention, shade the side below the line.

blocks.html: If the diagram shades the wanted side explicitly, read that side. In every case check the wording given.

examples.title: Choose how to draw the boundary
examples.question:
Which line style is used for the boundary of \(x+y\lt 2\)?

  1. Broken
  2. Solid
solution: Replace the sign with equality to get \(x+y=2\).
Use a broken boundary because equality is excluded.

examples.title: Read a vertical boundary
examples.question:
The shaded part is unwanted. Which inequality describes the clear half-plane?

  1. \(x\gt 2\)
  2. \(x\lt 2\)
  3. \(x\geq 2\)
  4. \(y\gt 2\)
solution: The vertical boundary has equation \(x=2\). Look at x-coordinates, which change left to right.
The clear side is to the right. Use the line type to get \(x\gt 2\).

examples.title: Read a horizontal boundary
examples.question:
Which condition describes the unshaded part of this graph?

  1. \(y\leq 1\)
  2. \(y\geq 1\)
  3. \(y\lt 1\)
  4. \(x\leq 1\)
solution: The horizontal boundary has equation \(y=1\).
The wanted area is below the boundary. The line style gives the inequality \(y\leq 1\).

examples.title: Use an off-line point to choose the side
examples.question:
For \(x+y\lt 2\), use \(\left(0,0\right)\) as a test point. Where does it lie?

  1. The test point is on the wanted side
  2. The test point is on the unwanted side
solution: The origin is off the line, so it can be used as a test point.
At \(\left(0,0\right)\), the left side has value \(0\). The comparison \(0\lt 2\) is true.
The test point is on the wanted side.

examples.title: Use an off-line point to choose the side
examples.question:
For \(x+y\lt 0\), use \(\left(1,1\right)\) as a test point. Where does it lie?

  1. The test point is on the wanted side
  2. The test point is on the unwanted side
solution: The origin is on this boundary, so choose another point.
At \(\left(1,1\right)\), the left side has value \(2\). The comparison \(2\lt 0\) is false.
The test point is on the unwanted side.

examples.title: Choose the unwanted side of a sloping boundary
examples.question:
For \(x+y\geq 3\), which side of the boundary should be shaded using the Cambridge convention?

  1. Above
  2. Below
solution: Isolate y in \(x+y\geq 3\). The wanted region is above the line.
With Cambridge's convention, shade the side below the line.

extraPractice.title: Choose how to draw the boundary
extraPractice.prompt: Which line style is used for the boundary of \(x+y\leq 4\)?
extraPractice.hint: A line style only tells whether the boundary itself belongs.
extraPractice.solution:
Replace the sign with equality to get \(x+y=4\).

Use a solid boundary because equality is allowed.

extraPractice.title: Read a vertical boundary
extraPractice.prompt: The shaded part is unwanted. Which inequality describes the clear half-plane?
extraPractice.hint: A vertical boundary limits x. Check which side is clear and whether the line is broken.
extraPractice.solution:
The vertical boundary has equation \(x=4\). Look at x-coordinates, which change left to right.

The clear side is to the left. Use the line type to get \(x\lt 4\).

extraPractice.title: Read a horizontal boundary
extraPractice.prompt: Which condition describes the unshaded part of this graph?
extraPractice.hint: In a horizontal boundary, the fixed coordinate is y.
extraPractice.solution:
The horizontal boundary has equation \(y=-1\).

The wanted area is below the boundary. The line style gives the inequality \(y\lt -1\).

extraPractice.title: Use an off-line point to choose the side
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x+y\leq 4\), use \(\left(0,0\right)\) as a test point. Where does it lie?
extraPractice.hint: Substitute both coordinates and decide whether the comparison is true.
extraPractice.solution:
The origin is off the line, so it can be used as a test point.

At \(\left(0,0\right)\), the left side has value \(0\). The comparison \(0\leq 4\) is true.

The test point is on the wanted side.

options.A: The test point is on the wanted side
options.B: The test point is on the unwanted side

extraPractice.title: Use an off-line point to choose the side
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x+y\leq 0\), use \(\left(1,1\right)\) as a test point. Where does it lie?
extraPractice.hint: Substitute both coordinates and decide whether the comparison is true.
extraPractice.solution:
The origin is on this boundary, so choose another point.

At \(\left(1,1\right)\), the left side has value \(2\). The comparison \(2\leq 0\) is false.

The test point is on the unwanted side.

options.A: The test point is on the wanted side
options.B: The test point is on the unwanted side

extraPractice.title: Choose the unwanted side of a sloping boundary
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x+y\leq 5\), which side of the boundary should be shaded using the Cambridge convention?
extraPractice.hint: First find the satisfying side. Shade the other one.
extraPractice.solution:
Isolate y in \(x+y\leq 5\). The wanted region is below the line.

With Cambridge's convention, shade the side above the line.

glossary.definition: The line obtained when the two expressions are equal.
One side of a line in a coordinate plane.
An off-line point substituted to identify the satisfying side.
An included boundary.
An excluded boundary.

revision.body:
Find the boundary and its style

Change the sign to equality to get the boundary. Use solid for \(\leq,\ \geq\) and broken for \(\lt,\ \gt\).

Test a point off the line

Substitute a point off the boundary. Shade the side where the inequality fails, unless told otherwise.

Read both direction and equality

Compare x across a vertical boundary and y across a horizontal boundary. For a sloping line, use a point or rearrange for y.

Example

For \(x+y\geq 3\), draw \(x+y=3\) solid. At the origin, 0 is smaller than 3, so shade the side containing the origin.

Check yourself

  • Is the boundary of \(x\lt 2\) solid or broken?
  • Which side of \(y=4\) is unwanted for \(y\geq 4\)?

Answers Broken, and below the horizontal line.
revision.checks:
• The style of the line does not tell you which side to shade. Make the side decision separately.
  • If the origin lies on the boundary, it cannot distinguish the two sides. Test a different easy point.
  • The visual edge of the printed grid is not a boundary of the inequality unless the question draws or states it as one.
revision.examTip: If the diagram shades the wanted side explicitly, read that side. In every case check the wording given.

igcse-0580-inequalities-graph-regions.description: Use the overlap of satisfying half-planes and list every inequality that defines a region.

sections.title: How do I draw the overlap of several conditions?
sections.label: Shade each unwanted half-plane
sections.intro: Draw the boundary for every inequality. Choose solid or broken separately for each. Then remove each unwanted half-plane by shading it.

blocks.html: Under the usual Cambridge convention, the clear part satisfies every condition. Label it R. You can test a point inside R in all the original inequalities.

figure.alt: The clear region R is right of a solid vertical line at x equal to 1, above a broken horizontal line at y equal to 1, and below a solid diagonal with both intercepts 6.
figure.caption: R remains clear after three unwanted half-planes have been shaded. The broken lower boundary is excluded.

blocks.title: List all inequalities that define the region
blocks.prompt: The area marked R is left clear. Choose the list of inequalities defining R.
blocks.hint: Find each boundary equation first. Then use the location of R and the line style to choose its inequality.
blocks.solution:
Compare x to the vertical line \(x=2\). The line type and position of R give \(x\geq 2\).

Compare y to the horizontal line \(y=2\). The line type and position of R give \(y\lt 2\).

Compare an interior point with the sloping line \(x+y=5\). The line type and position of R give \(x+y\leq 5\).

All of these restrictions must hold together: \(x\geq 2\), \(y\lt 2\), \(x+y\leq 5\).

blocks.html: Even if a point passes two conditions, it belongs outside R if it fails a third. Find the overlap, not a single satisfying half-plane.

blocks.title: List all inequalities that define the region
blocks.prompt: The area marked R is left clear. Choose the list of inequalities defining R.
blocks.hint: Find each boundary equation first. Then use the location of R and the line style to choose its inequality.
blocks.solution:
Compare x to the vertical line \(x=1\). The line type and position of R give \(x\gt 1\).

Compare an interior point with the sloping line \(-x+y=1\). The line type and position of R give \(-x+y\leq 1\).

Compare an interior point with the sloping line \(x+y=5\). The line type and position of R give \(x+y\lt 5\).

All of these restrictions must hold together: \(x\gt 1\), \(-x+y\leq 1\), \(x+y\lt 5\).

blocks.html: Draw the boundary lines first. Test and shade one boundary at a time.

sections.title: Which inequalities define the region shown?
sections.label: Identify each line and read inwards
sections.intro: Read the shape's boundary lines from their intercepts or points. If needed, use two visible points to find the gradient of a sloping line.

blocks.html: For each line, choose a point strictly inside R to determine the sign. Then use the line style to decide about equality. List all the conditions together.

blocks.title: List all inequalities that define the region
blocks.prompt: In this question the wanted region R is shaded. Choose the list of inequalities defining R.
blocks.hint: Find each boundary equation first. Then use the location of R and the line style to choose its inequality.
blocks.solution:
Compare x to the vertical line \(x=2\). The line type and position of R give \(x\geq 2\).

Compare y to the horizontal line \(y=3\). The line type and position of R give \(y\gt 3\).

All of these restrictions must hold together: \(x\geq 2\), \(y\gt 3\).

blocks.html: The shaded side is normally unwanted. If a question explicitly shades R itself, interpret the shaded part as wanted for that question.

blocks.title: Test every inequality before accepting a point
blocks.prompt: Which point satisfies all the conditions \(x\geq 2\), \(y\lt 2\), \(x+y\leq 5\)?
blocks.hint: A point must pass every condition. Read strict and inclusive signs carefully.
blocks.solution:
Check x and y first. The first boundary accepts the selected point with \(x=2\). The y-coordinate is \(1\), which is strictly below \(2\).

The sum of its coordinates is \(3\) and satisfies \(x+y\leq 5\). Thus \(\left(2,1\right)\) meets all the conditions.

blocks.html: An equivalent rearrangement of an inequality describes the same region if the sign reverses when you divide by a negative.

sections.title: How do I check points on a boundary or corner?
sections.label: Apply all boundary conditions
sections.intro: Test a boundary point against every condition. An included point may lie on a solid boundary if it satisfies the rest of the system.

blocks.html: A point on any broken line fails the strict inequality for that line. A corner only counts if all adjacent boundaries allow equality and every other condition is true.

blocks.title: Test every inequality before accepting a point
blocks.prompt: Which point satisfies all the conditions \(x\gt 2\), \(y\lt 2\), \(x+y\leq 5\)?
blocks.hint: A point must pass every condition. Read strict and inclusive signs carefully.
blocks.solution:
Check x and y first. The first boundary accepts the selected point with \(x=3\). The y-coordinate is \(1\), which is strictly below \(2\).

The sum of its coordinates is \(4\) and satisfies \(x+y\leq 5\). Thus \(\left(3,1\right)\) meets all the conditions.

blocks.html: An unshaded segment drawn with breaks is an excluded boundary. The line style still matters after shading.

blocks.title: Shade each unwanted side and look for the common region
blocks.prompt: To show the region where \(x\geq 2\), \(y\gt 3\) all hold, what should you do at the vertical boundary?
blocks.hint: For the vertical line, first compare a smaller x-value with the stated bound. Shade the side that fails.
blocks.solution:
The vertical boundary is \(x=2\). The x-values to its left fail the condition.

Shade the left of the vertical boundary, the side disallowed by the horizontal boundary. The overlap of the wanted sides is clear.

options.A: Shade to the right of x = 2.
options.C: Shade to the left of x = 2.

blocks.html: Give the full list of inequalities for the region. An example point alone does not define it.

examples.title: List all inequalities that define the region
examples.question:
The area marked R is left clear. Choose the list of inequalities defining R.

  1. \(x\geq 1\), \(y\lt 1\), \(x+y\leq 4\)
  2. \(x\leq 1\), \(y\lt 1\), \(x+y\leq 4\)
  3. \(x\geq 1\), \(y\gt 1\), \(x+y\leq 4\)
  4. \(x\geq 1\), \(y\lt 1\), \(x+y\geq 4\)
solution: Compare x to the vertical line \(x=1\). The line type and position of R give \(x\geq 1\).
Compare y to the horizontal line \(y=1\). The line type and position of R give \(y\lt 1\).
Compare an interior point with the sloping line \(x+y=4\). The line type and position of R give \(x+y\leq 4\).
All of these restrictions must hold together: \(x\geq 1\), \(y\lt 1\), \(x+y\leq 4\).

examples.title: List all inequalities that define the region
examples.question:
The area marked R is left clear. Choose the list of inequalities defining R.

  1. \(x\gt 0\), \(-x+y\leq 1\), \(x+y\lt 4\)
  2. \(x\lt 0\), \(-x+y\leq 1\), \(x+y\lt 4\)
  3. \(x\gt 0\), \(-x+y\geq 1\), \(x+y\lt 4\)
  4. \(x\gt 0\), \(-x+y\leq 1\), \(x+y\gt 4\)
solution: Compare x to the vertical line \(x=0\). The line type and position of R give \(x\gt 0\).
Compare an interior point with the sloping line \(-x+y=1\). The line type and position of R give \(-x+y\leq 1\).
Compare an interior point with the sloping line \(x+y=4\). The line type and position of R give \(x+y\lt 4\).
All of these restrictions must hold together: \(x\gt 0\), \(-x+y\leq 1\), \(x+y\lt 4\).

examples.title: List all inequalities that define the region
examples.question:
In this question the wanted region R is shaded. Choose the list of inequalities defining R.

  1. \(x\geq 1\), \(y\gt 2\)
  2. \(x\leq 1\), \(y\gt 2\)
  3. \(x\geq 1\), \(y\lt 2\)
  4. \(x\geq 1\), \(y\geq 2\)
solution: Compare x to the vertical line \(x=1\). The line type and position of R give \(x\geq 1\).
Compare y to the horizontal line \(y=2\). The line type and position of R give \(y\gt 2\).
All of these restrictions must hold together: \(x\geq 1\), \(y\gt 2\).

examples.title: Test every inequality before accepting a point
examples.question:
Which point satisfies all the conditions \(x\geq 1\), \(y\lt 1\), \(x+y\leq 4\)?

  1. \(\left(1,0\right)\)
  2. \(\left(0,0\right)\)
  3. \(\left(1,1\right)\)
  4. \(\left(2,2\right)\)
solution: Check x and y first. The first boundary accepts the selected point with \(x=1\). The y-coordinate is \(0\), which is strictly below \(1\).
The sum of its coordinates is \(1\) and satisfies \(x+y\leq 4\). Thus \(\left(1,0\right)\) meets all the conditions.

examples.title: Test every inequality before accepting a point
examples.question:
Which point satisfies all the conditions \(x\gt 1\), \(y\lt 1\), \(x+y\leq 4\)?

  1. \(\left(2,0\right)\)
  2. \(\left(0,0\right)\)
  3. \(\left(1,1\right)\)
  4. \(\left(2,2\right)\)
solution: Check x and y first. The first boundary accepts the selected point with \(x=2\). The y-coordinate is \(0\), which is strictly below \(1\).
The sum of its coordinates is \(2\) and satisfies \(x+y\leq 4\). Thus \(\left(2,0\right)\) meets all the conditions.

examples.title: Shade each unwanted side and look for the common region
examples.question:
To show the region where \(x\geq 1\), \(y\lt 1\), \(x+y\leq 4\) all hold, what should you do at the vertical boundary?

  1. Shade to the left of x = 1.
  2. Shade to the right of x = 1.
  3. Leave both sides unshaded.
solution: The vertical boundary is \(x=1\). The x-values to its left fail the condition.
Shade the left of the vertical boundary, the side disallowed by the horizontal boundary and the area above the descending line. The overlap of the wanted sides is clear.

glossary.definition: A set of points in the coordinate plane.
Points of a region that are not on its edge.
Several conditions that must all hold together.
Where a line meets one of the axes.
The intersection of two boundary lines.

revision.body:
Shade each unwanted half-plane

Shade each unwanted side. Label the clear overlap R.

Identify each line and read inwards

Find each line's equation. A point inside R gives the sign. The line style gives the equality decision.

Apply all boundary conditions

A point belongs to R only when every condition holds. Points on a broken boundary are excluded.

Example

In this diagram, R satisfies \(x\geq 1\), \(y\gt 1\) and \(x+y\leq 6\).

Check yourself

  • Does \((1,2)\) belong to the region R in the diagram?
  • Does \((2,1)\) belong to that region?

Answers Yes, and no. The second point is on the excluded lower boundary.
revision.checks:
• Even if a point passes two conditions, it belongs outside R if it fails a third. Find the overlap, not a single satisfying half-plane.
  • The shaded side is normally unwanted. If a question explicitly shades R itself, interpret the shaded part as wanted for that question.
  • An unshaded segment drawn with breaks is an excluded boundary. The line style still matters after shading.
revision.examTip: Give the full list of inequalities for the region. An example point alone does not define it.
